rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.2, two-year (2017-2018) split-plot field experiment in a commercial Cabernet Sauvignon vineyard, Red Mountain AVA, WA. Q2: Section 3.5 and Table 3, irrigation method had a significant effect on yield in both years, with about 9% (2017) and 12% (2018) higher yield under DRZ than SD across all rates (10.0 vs 9.2 and 10.4 vs 9.3 t/ha). Q4: Section 3.3, Fig. 3 and Table 1, midday stem water potential measured by pressure chamber was 10-14% higher under DRZ after veraison in both years; Discussion links lower water stress to more resources for yield. Q8: Section 5 and Discussion, authors state that reduced soil evaporation and deep rooting as reasons for the DRZ effect remain untested, that roots were observed only to 60 cm, that no PVC effect on soil was assumed, and that a long-term (e.g. 10-year) study is needed to evaluate benefits and define conditions.
rows.notes: Yield measured by one method (hand harvest weighing) only. Single site, single soil (Hezel loamy fine sand), single cultivar; two years with differing weather but not distinct climates. Plot scale (15-vine plots) within a commercial vineyard, not farm/district scale. Soil-texture conditions are discussed from literature, not own findings. Table 3 gives means and Tukey letters only, no SD/SE/CI for yield.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.2, own two-year field experiment (2017-2018) with three irrigation rates x two methods in three blocks. Q2: Section 3.5, 3.6 and Table 3, DRZ increased grape yield by about 9% and 12% and WUEc by 9-11% relative to SD in both years, with significant method effects and no rate x method interaction. Q4: Section 3.3, Fig. 3, Table 1, midday stem water potential (plant water status) measured as the intermediate variable, 10-14% higher under DRZ after veraison in both years. Q8: Section 5 and Discussion end, mechanisms (reduced evaporation, deep root development) stated as untested and needing future study; root imaging restricted to 0-60 cm; long-term study needed to evaluate economic and environmental benefits and optimum conditions.
rows.notes: 'Varied climate conditions' in the passage refers only to two contrasting years at one site; not multiple climates/regions. Yield and WUEc from a single method (harvest weighing plus metered irrigation and rain). No dispersion measure reported for yield or WUEc in Table 3 (means with letters only). Support factors not stated as requirements from own data.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.8, own two-year field experiment with measured irrigation amounts (water meters) and harvested yield. Q2: Section 3.6 and Table 3, WUEc (yield per mm irrigation plus rainfall) significantly affected by method in both years, DRZ improved WUEc by 9-11% compared to SD (38.3 vs 35.1 and 43.8 vs 39.3 kg/ha/mm). Q4: Section 3.3 and Fig. 3, midday stem water potential measured as the plant water-status intermediate, significantly higher under DRZ post-veraison, which the authors link to more available water. Q8: Section 5, authors state that reduced soil water evaporation as the cause of the DRZ advantage needs testing in future studies, and that a long-term study is needed to define desirable conditions for DRZ.
rows.notes: WUEc computed from a single method; soil evaporation or soil water content under the two methods was not measured, so the water-conservation mechanism is inferred (Q4 'yes' rests on measured stem water potential only). Single site/soil/crop; plot scale. No SD/SE for WUEc in Table 3.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.6, own field experiment with pressure-chamber stem water potential and minirhizotron root imaging over two seasons. Q2: Section 3.3, Fig. 3 and Table 1, under seasonal deficit (rainfall extremely limited from fruit set to harvest) DRZ vines had significantly 10-14% higher midday stem water potential than SD after veraison in both years, i.e. less water stress; Section 3.5 and Table 4, berry weight, diameter and number were modified by irrigation rate. Q8: Section 5 and Discussion, authors state that deep root development below 60 cm and reduced evaporation as explanations are untested, root observation was limited to the 0-60 cm profile, and a long-term study is required.
rows.notes: The 'deep rooting' part of the claim is an inference: roots below 60 cm were not observed; the study only measured fewer roots in 0-60 cm under DRZ and inferred deeper rooting. Hence the mechanism is asserted, not measured (Q4 no). Water stress alleviation evidenced by one method (stem water potential). Fig. 3 caption reports n=9 and Tukey letters but no dispersion measure is mentioned for stem water potential; root figures (Figs 4, 6, 7) show SE bars but those are not the claimed effect. Single site, plot scale, no requirement conditions stated from own data.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references); supplementary figures/tables not available. Table 2 layout is garbled in the extraction but values are readable. DRZ is a subsurface drip variant delivering water through vertical PVC tubes, treated as matching the 'drip' technology field. Note that the passage for rows 2-4 says DRZ was contrasted with 'SDI', whereas the study compares DRZ with surface drip (SD); treated as a wording slip, not a technology mismatch.
